Checking the Distributor Cap: The Cause of Engine Misfires

Engine misfires may be a frustrating experience for any vehicle owner. The unexpected jerk, lack of power, and harsh idle might leave you wondering what's causing it. A defective distributor cap is one of the most prevalent causes of engine misfires. Understanding the function of the distributor cap and how to inspect it will help you save time and money on repairs.
What is the Distributor Cap?

The distributor cap is critical to your vehicle's ignition system. It delivers high voltage from the ignition coil to the spark plugs in the proper firing order. This process ignites the air-fuel combination in the engine cylinders, allowing your vehicle to operate smoothly. Over time, the distributor cap may wear out, break, or corrode, resulting in engine misfire.
Signs of a Faulty Distributor Cap

A misfiring engine frequently indicates an issue with the ignition system. If your engine misfires, particularly when accelerating or under load, it might be due to a malfunctioning distributor cap. A rough or uneven idle might indicate that the spark is not evenly spread across the engine's cylinders. Furthermore, a broken distributor cap might create difficulty starting the vehicle, especially in damp or rainy weather. Cracks, carbon tracks, and corrosion on the distributor cap are all obvious symptoms of wear and strain.
How to Check the Distributor Cap?

Start by physically scrutinizing the distributor cap. Look for cracks, carbon tracks, and corrosion. If you see any damage, replace the cap. To have a closer look, remove the distributor cap. This usually entails releasing a few screws or clips. Inside the cap, there are metal contacts. Inspect for excessive wear, pitting, or corrosion. Clean the contacts if they are unclean
column2:
if they are broken, replace the cap. While the cap is off, check the rotor for similar indications of wear. If the rotor and distributor cap are damaged, they should be replaced.

If you notice indications of a malfunctioning distributor cap, conduct a thorough check and replace it as needed. Keeping your vehicle's ignition system in good working order is critical to preserving its performance and dependability.

Diagnose a Bad AC: an Easy DIY for GM Vehicles

There's nothing worse than to be on the road in the heat of a North Carolina summer and have the air conditioner go out. After all, it doesn't just cool the interior during a drive. It also keeps the seats, armrests, and steering wheel comfortable enough to the touch not to burn you when you get in for a drive.

The thing is, when car AC systems do fail, the cause could be anything -- the compressor, condenser, the evaporator, refrigerant levels, even just a weakened seal or a degraded or broken hose. Here's how to tell what the problem might be.
Low Refrigerant
Your Buick Enclave, for instance, doesn't cool properly, and usually, the cause is low refrigerant -- either levels are a problem, or there's a leak. You can figure out which.

Start your engine, set the AC to max cool, set the fans on their highest setting, and listen for the compressor clutch to click on. If it seems like it's working too fast, refrigerant's likely low. If it's not due for service, a leak's likely. What you want to do is check all the seals -- the fittings, the compressor hose manifolds, the hoses themselves (at the fittings), the front seal and O-rings (these seal the compressor's pressure switches), the Schrader valves, and where condensation drains out the evaporator. Also, check the condenser for pinholes. Replace whatever you need to.
AC Compressor Failure

Interior of, say, your Cadillac XT5 warmer than usual? You can chalk that up to compressor problems, most of the time. Weird noises from it, the clutch getting stuck -- these make it pretty much official. How to tell if you've got a bad clutch is simple: connect a voltmeter. No voltage, the clutch is likely failed. Other issues could be a faulty cycling switch, a blown fuse, or low refrigerant pressure. Replace whatever's not working.
Faulty AC Condenser

An SUV like Chevy Traverse or GMC Acadia, you might also run into things like frost accumulation, with a flashing AC button and a lit HVAC warning light to boot. You might even notice discharge pressure issues. These almost always mean condenser trouble.

Here's how to tell. Start the engine, max out the AC, put the fans on high, and check the air coming through the vents. If it's not that cool, the condenser's likely to blame. (Of course, if no air's moving at all, the blower motor is likely bad.) You'll want to check the cooling fans on the condenser and radiator to make sure they're working, and look for any dirt or debris clogging the airflow in the condenser area -- specifically, the condenser vents to the outside. Also, check the cabin air filter for clogs. Again, replace any problem parts.
Of course, if you're not sure what to do, a GM dealer or an authorized GM service center would be glad to help.

Carburetors' Primary Functions and Mechanisms

Carburetors combine air and fuel properly in an internal combustion engine. GM carburetors are engineered to accurately regulate this combination, resulting in improved engine performance, fuel efficiency, and emissions management.

The carburetor starts by pulling air via an air filter. This air flows through a constriction called a venturi, which increases its velocity while decreasing its pressure. The venturi's lower pressure takes fuel from the float chamber through a jet, where it mixes with the incoming air. The form and size of the venturi and jet are regulated to achieve the proper air-fuel ratio. A throttle valve, operated by the accelerator pedal, regulates the quantity of air-fuel mixture that enters the engine. When the throttle is opened, more air-fuel mixture enters the engine, which boosts power production. The mixture is then atomized and evaporated as it travels through the intake manifold, resulting in full combustion in the engine cylinders.
Air Filters’ Primary Functions and Mechanisms

Air cleaners safeguard the engine by filtering out dust, grime, and other impurities before they enter the carburetor. Air cleaners catch particles using filter media, commonly comprised of paper, foam, or cotton. This prevents pollutants from entering the carburetor or engine. They are intended to offer maximum airflow while ensuring excellent filtering efficiency. Proper airflow is required for the carburetor to maintain the right air-fuel ratio. Regular maintenance and replacement of air filters are essential. A blocked air filter can reduce airflow, causing the engine to run rich (consuming too much gasoline) and lowering performance and fuel economy.

Why an Air Cleaner Should be Your Next Chevy Engine Mod

Your Chevy vehicle's built for performance
column23:

You've got plenty of choices. Drive an everyday car, a pleated paper air cleaner should do
column24:
it's designed easy enough to replace, and cost-effective, too. Got a sports car or another performance vehicle, though -- a truck like Chevy Silverado 1500 or an SUV like Chevy Tahoe -- and foam and cotton air cleaners are good choices. Foam ones use long-lasting oil-wetted polyurethane -- you see them a lot in motorsports -- and cotton ones use oiled gauze. You get great airflow from both, and with high dirt capacities to boot. Of course, if you're an off-roader, with a vehicle like Chevy Trailblazer, an oil bath air cleaner is probably your best bet. Their oil sumps and coarse inserts -- made of fiber, mesh, or foam -- give you the best filtration you can get.

Whatever air cleaner you choose, just be sure to regularly inspect it to make sure it lasts the 12,000 to 15,000 miles that it should. Just as importantly, keep an eye out for signs it's going bad -- a Check Engine light or another warning light on the dash, worsening gas mileage, ignition problems, unusual engine noises, and the like. Find it damaged or dirty, and it's probably time to replace it -- the filter itself, at least, if not the whole assembly.

What Does a Bed Liner Do for a Chevy or GMC Pickup?

Basically, it does what a cargo liner and cargo tray does for the bare floor plastics and upholstery in a car or SUV. It helps keep muck and debris from collecting in and on the truck box, which damage it and eventually rust out its metals. They also shield the bed from the bumps and scrapes caused by cargo prone to shifting during transport -- power tools, big equipment, building materials, and the like.

What Types of Bed Liners are There?

Drop-in and spray-on are the commonest. Drop-in bed liners do as they seem -- they drop in place in the truck bed, and they're removable. Most are made of plastic. Spray-on bed liners are typically an aliphatic or polyurethane base applied with a spray gun, but you can sometimes paint them on with a brush instead. (Roll-on bed liners are similar to the latter -- they apply to the surfaces of truck boxes with a paint roller.) Both protect a truck in the long term, as they're supposed to be permanent solutions.

There are other kinds of bed liners, too, most notably those that come in several parts that you lock together. Carpet bed liners, though, attach using hook and loop fastener, most of the time, and they can cover either the bottom of truck boxes only or their entirety. Disposable and portable truck bed liners, for another example, are a temporary type. The former is for one-time use, while the latter can last for several hauls. There are also such things as rubber bed mats, but they're different from bed liners insofar as they don't replace them per se
column2:
however, they do serve as additional protective layers, and durable ones at that.

Why Buy Genuine GM Bed Liners?

GM designs them compatible with your pickup truck specifically, whether you drive a Chevy Colorado, a GMC Canyon, or otherwise. Aftermarket bed liners can't always make the same guarantee. Even if one does, it still may not fit quite right or function as it should.

What Do Fog Lights Do for GM Vehicles?

The shine low, wide, and brightly with short beams. This makes them ideal for lighting the way in bad weather where visibility's limited. In fact, they do this much better than your average headlights and taillights do.

What Types of Fog Lights are There?

There are three: halogen, Xenon (also called high-intensity discharge/HID), and LED. Halogen fog lights are the commonest
column2:

When Do You Replace Fog Lights?

Halogen fog light bulbs, you should change every couple of years or so. Change HID fog light bulbs, on the other hand, as they weaken
